newsitem.title: UK: Commodities - Investors need to pick and choose. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Commodities - Investors need to pick and choose. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]

text.p: Commodity markets have had a volatile start to 1997 but fund managers and analysts say investors should expect steady rewards rather than thrills as the year progresses, citing only modest global economic expansion.

"I think in commodities it's going to be a selective game. Some sectors will perform and others won't. It's a matter of getting into the right sector," said Robin Edwards, director of Sabre Wolff fund management.
Among the commodities other than petroleum, investors have already jumped in to coffee which soared 30 percent this month on fears of a low crop in Brazil.
London futures for robusta coffee seemed poised to extend gains toward $1,650 a tonne from $1,480 now.

Metals also saw higher fund exposure on expectations that raw material demand will rise as economic activity accelerates. But that may be delayed if policymakers respond to signs of inflation by raising interest rates.
Commodities will also be at the whim of an uncertain Japanese economy and from spending cuts in European Union countries that need to meet fiscal criteria to join a single currency.
But the commodity markets may be the beneficiaries if there is an exodus of hot money from "toppy" stocks and bonds.
"Funds that invest in bonds and equities might think that those markets have little scope now to appreciate," said Robin Bhar, metals analyst at Brandeis.
Sabre's Edwards said that the jury was out on whether signs of flattening U.S. bond prices heralded a surge in metals prices just yet.
"You are not seeing this confirmation of bullishness in bonds, but that can change very quickly," Edwards said. "If I had a choice, I would rather be long of base metals and short of bonds".
In metals, investors singled out zinc, aluminium and nickel as the likely winners after a de-stocking in the last two years.
But the bellwether copper was least favoured, despite a recent rally, while the market remained burdened by rising production and concerns about the Sumitomo scandal.

Metals analysts said that blips up were possible from the current London Metal Exchange copper price around $2,150-2,160 (corrects from $2,150-7560), with the level of Chinese buying likely to be a deciding factor.

"Towards the top of ranking would be zinc. It has lagged behind the other metals pressured by high stocks in the last years but those are coming down because there is a structural deficit," said Bhar.
Three-month zinc has peaked at $1,160 a tonne on LME in January and analysts expected a spike towards $1,300 on buoyant demand.
Aluminium would track demand-inspired growth despite large supplies waiting in the wings, while the rise in nickel might be moderated by slower growth cycles in stainless steel.
Investors polled by Reuters last month saw aluminium averaging at $1,754 a tonne this year from $1,620 now.
Prospects in gold look less rosy, according to Tony Warwick-Ching, precious metals consultant at CRU International.

Investors fled out of bullion earlier this month in the wake of Dutch central bank sales of 300 tonnes of gold -- and more such sales are thought to be in the pipeline as the precious metal loses its role as reserve asset.
Bullion tumbled below the key $350 an ounce level this week and was seen extending its slide to $340, a significant support level from 1993.
"I don't think it will go a lot lower but it's hard to see what can turn this," said Warwick-Ching.
A strong dollar, low inflation and a surge in stocks took the shine off bullion while Japan, traditionally a major importer, has reined back its purchases due to the weak yen.
"Buyers have come back to lower prices but there isn't that extra zip in demand," said Warwick-Ching, who saw gold at $350.00-$365 short-term.
Silver could rally but may find it difficult to sustain gains, while platinum could wait for gold to recover, analysts said.
In soft commodities, coffee's fortunes hinged on a possible poor harvest in Brazil and the implementation of export cuts agreed this month by key producers, market sources said.

Cocoa languishes around 900 pounds sterling a tonne in London, but it too could be kickstarted if top grower Ivory Coast gathers a smaller than expected crop. Arrival rates so far point to an ample harvest.
Players will also monitor moves by one trade house that controls a large chunk of world supplies delivered to it after a squeeze in September.
Sugar and grains are seen looking for further dips.
"Grains are most probably in some form of bear market, unless we get some major supply shock," said Edwards of Sabre Wolff.
Argentina and Australia undercut world prices with aggressive exports just as key importers saw an upturn in their own production this year, relying less on imports.

"Although India came into the (import) picture, that probably will be counteracted by lower figures in China," said Bill de Maria, assistant executive director of the International Grains Council (IGC).

But stocks are still recovering from 20-year lows that threatened supplies last year, and the price of wheat - now around $3.70 a bushel in Chicago after above $7.00 last year - remains vulnerable to weather problems. -- London Newsroom +44-171-542 8072
